name: PT Resource Alam Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Resource Alam Indonesia — a non-coal asset floor under a low-grade coal producer
frontmatter.summary: KKGI is a small, tightly held low-calorific coal miner whose market value sits close to its net cash plus its non-coal assets. Output was cut to defend margin, the dividend has exceeded earnings, and most of the leadership was replaced this year. The balance sheet supports the price; the coal business adds only a thin, front-loaded layer of value. We initiate at BUY with a Rp374 target, a 34.0% total return.
thesis: The market capitalisation is close to the sum of net cash and the book value of the non-coal assets — the Rain Realty land, the tax-refund claim, the restricted deposits, the long-term investment and the acquisition advances — so the coal business is being valued at less than nothing; that floor, not a coal-price recovery, is what supports the rating [S3][S4].

The product is low-calorific thermal coal, medium-grade but well below the benchmark, sold about half domestically, so it prices off a deep discount to the Newcastle marker; we calibrate realisation at a stable fraction of that marker across the last two actual years rather than fitting it to the current war-premium print [S2][S3].

Volume now follows the company's own reduced plan, not the historical capacity, because management explicitly chose margin over tonnes in a weak price year and is executing that plan in the first half [S2][S4].

The royalty is the rate the audited accounts show being paid and the rate written into the IBP contract of work, so the model reproduces the last actual year's EBITDA instead of over-charging the state take [S3].

Three directors left within a month and a new president director was appointed, while the controlling family and a single institutional holder own most of the register and the free float sits near the exchange minimum; governance and liquidity, not geology, are the binding constraints on the rating [S2][S8][S9][S10].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Resource Alam Indonesia Tbk, the IDX-listed low-calorific coal producer that trades as KKGI, at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp374 against a last price of Rp288 — an expected total return of 34.0%, of which 29.9% is price upside and the balance is the modelled dividend stream [S3][S4]. The call is not a bet on coal prices recovering. It is a bet that a company which owns a net-cash balance sheet, a land bank held at cost, a tax-refund claim, a portfolio of non-coal assets and a licence running to 2036 is worth at least the sum the market currently pays for it, with the coal business supplying a thin, front-loaded layer of value on top. The rating is BUY because the fully valued balance sheet — not the coal forecast — carries the target; the coal layer is small and the profit outlook uncertain, which is why the margin is not wider.

The variant view is about *what the market is capitalising*. KKGI is not a Newcastle producer and should never be priced as one. Its coal is medium-grade thermal coal — several thousand kilocalories per kilogram, well below the benchmark — sold about half into the domestic market and the rest to China and India [S2][S3]. It realises a deep discount to the six-thousand kcal marker — 41.3 dollars a tonne in FY2025 against a Newcastle average of 108.4 dollars [S2][S3]. At the deck's long-run Newcastle marker the mine is marginal: FY2025 EBIT was only US$5.7m on US$153.1m of revenue, and at the long-run anchor the realised price sits close to the H1-2026-evidenced cash cost plus royalty and SG&A [S3][S4]. The coal enterprise value our DCF supports is only 13.7 million dollars, a fraction of the market capitalisation; almost all of the equity value is the balance sheet. That is why the call is a balance-sheet call first and a coal call second — not because we assume a trough, but because the margin is genuinely thin. The value that the DCF captures sits on the balance sheet: cash of 44.7 million dollars against bank loans of 2.0 million and lease liabilities of 0.32 million current plus 0.27 million non-current at 30 June 2026, investment properties of 31.5 million dollars carried at cost, almost all of it land, a 10.3 million dollar estimated tax-refund claim carried at a discount for timing and collectability, a 2.7 million dollar long-term investment in non-controlled companies, 5.5 million dollars of restricted time deposits pledged against reclamation and IUP guarantees, and 3.4 million dollars of advances toward coal-company acquisitions — every one of them outside the coal DCF [S4].

The second leg is the cash return, and we model the recurring payout rather than the FY2025 one-off. The base carries a dividend of Rp12 a share, a yield of 4.1% on the current price, at the normal-year payout of 34.0% — the average of the two years before the FY2025 catch-up, FY2023 and FY2024, whose distributions were a fraction of earnings [S3]. The FY2025 distribution was well above that year's parent profit and was funded from retained cash [S10][S5]; we treat it as a catch-up distribution, not a policy, and do not capitalise it as a perpetuity. That still pays a minority holder while owning an illiquid stock, but it does not carry the rating on its own.

The third leg is the option value that we deliberately keep out of the base case. The coal contract runs to 2036 and the reserve base would support production well beyond it, so a licence extension is worth something we do not pay for; the large East Kalimantan land bank behind Rain Realty is carried at cost and could be developed; and the company has begun spending on new-mine exploration [S2][S5]. None of that is in the target. We carry it as upside and say so.

What moves the value is therefore narrow and identifiable: the Newcastle marker (through the calibrated realisation), the strip ratio (through unit cash cost), and the pace at which the net cash is distributed rather than dissipated. The bear case is a full unwind of the war premium, a mirrored RKAB/quota shock to volume and a deeper pit; on the fully valued balance sheet it values the equity at Rp332 before the house liquidity discount — above today's price, because the price already sits close to the book value of assets the company owns, so the bear is a protection case rather than a loss of capital. The genuine loss case is not a coal-price case: it is one in which the balance-sheet assets themselves prove unrealisable, which we flag in the risks section rather than hide in the base [S4]. The base case — the company's volume and price plan at the deck's mean-reverting path and the audited cost base — is Rp376. The bull case is the premium persisting and the company executing its lower cost plan at the 5.7x strip ratio it guides, with volumes well above plan but still below what the company sold in FY2025; we give it only a tail weight because it requires several things to go right at once, and even then it lifts the probability-weighted value to Rp416 rather than dominating the target [S0][S2].

PT Resource Alam Indonesia Tbk is an Indonesian coal producer listed on the IDX under the ticker KKGI. It was founded in 1981 as a wood-adhesive manufacturer, changed its name from PT Kurnia Kapuas Utama Tbk in 2003 and shifted its focus to coal, and today reports four main business segments — coal mining, wholesale of fuels, real estate and holding-company activities — with coal providing almost all of the economics [S2]. The consolidated revenue base is small: total revenue was US$153.1m in FY2025, of which coal sales were the overwhelming majority and non-coal revenue, including electricity from a mini-hydro plant and property income, was a small residual [S3].

The operating heart is PT Insani Baraperkasa, which holds a third-generation coal contract of work (CCoW) over more than twenty-four thousand hectares in East Kalimantan and has produced since 2006 [S2][S3]. The contract entitles IBP to the large majority of coal produced, with the balance the Government's production share, which the company settles as a sales-based royalty inside cost of revenue [S3]. Within that contract the company works several exploitation areas — Simpang Pasir, Bayur, Tani Bakti, Gunung Pinang, Loajanan, Separi and Perangat — and the reserve table is reported by area [S4]. Two smaller licences sit alongside it: PT Kaltim Mineral holds an IUP operation- production licence over ten thousand hectares with lower-calorific coal, and PT Loa Haur holds an IUP in Central Kalimantan still at an early exploration stage [S2].

The product is medium-grade thermal coal in the low-to-mid four thousands of kilocalories per kilogram, marketed through an integrated approach that balances domestic offtake against export opportunities [S2]. That grade explains the business's economics. It is not a high-energy metallurgical or premium thermal product; it competes for power-station and industrial demand where price per calorie matters more than brand, and its realised price therefore sits far below the Newcastle benchmark. In FY2025 domestic customers took 77.8 million dollars of the US$153.1m revenue, with China and India the largest export destinations [S3].

Strategy in the most recent year has been defensive rather than expansionary. Management cut the production plan to focus on lower-cost mining areas, reduced the stripping ratio, and explicitly framed 2026 as a year of cost efficiency, operational stability and measured diversification rather than aggressive growth [S2]. Alongside coal it is developing the Rain Realty property segment on a land bank of several thousand hectares in East Kalimantan, operating a mini-hydro plant at Cicatih, and exploring a second hydro project at Bener Dam [S2]. These are small relative to coal but they are real assets and they are why the balance sheet carries investment properties at a meaningful value.

KKGI is a challenger by size, not a leader. National coal output was close to eight hundred million tonnes in 2025 according to the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, and KKGI's production of 3.6 million tonnes is a fraction of one percent of that [S2]. Its advantage is not scale but position: a domestic customer base, an established contractor-operated mine, and a contract that runs to 2036 [S3]. The controlling shareholder is PT Sejahtera Jaya Cita with 27.8% of the shares, held for the Adjianto family, alongside a stake of roughly a third held through UBS Singapore for Energy Collier Pte Ltd, a further holding of about eight per cent by Sinar Nusantara and a strategic stake of about five per cent held by Korea's LX International [S2]. The public holds the rest, and treasury stock accounts for a small slice [S2].

Indonesian thermal coal is a large, mature export industry that is being deliberately constrained at home. National production reached close to eight hundred million tonnes in 2025, of which about a third was used domestically and roughly two-thirds exported, with the balance retained as stock [S2]. The government manages the industry through an annual work-plan and budget quota (RKAB), the domestic market obligation (DMO), a progressive royalty regime and, since 2025, retention rules on export proceeds. In 2026 the state cut the RKAB to around six hundred million tonnes and then partially reopened it, but only for volumes destined for the state utility: the July 2026 revision added supply exclusively for PLN, with medium-to-high calorific coal of 4,500 kcal and above allocated to the Java system [S6]. That policy matters for KKGI in both directions. It supports domestic demand for its grade, but it also shows how quickly a quota decision can change a producer's addressable market.

The price backdrop is a war premium layered on a structurally softening market. The reviewed coal deck puts the Newcastle six-thousand marker at 108.4 dollars a tonne for FY2025, rising to 137.0 dollars in the current year on the war-premium bid and Chinese supply curbs, then mean-reverting to 118.0 and 105.0 dollars, with a long-run anchor of 105.0 dollars [S0]. Spot sits above the forward path at 150.3 dollars, which the desk treats as cycle position rather than value. The grade structure tells the same story: in the October 2026 government reference prices, high-calorific coal printed at 126.8 dollars, 4,100 kcal coal at 66.1 dollars and 3,400 kcal coal at 45.5 dollars, with the lower grades rising faster than the high grade from their July levels [S7]. The spread is the market's statement that the scarcity is in high-energy coal, not in the low-grade end where KKGI sits.

Our model prices KKGI off the Newcastle marker rather than the grade-matched HBA series, because only the Newcastle deck carries a reviewed forward through-cycle path; HBA II is a spot print. That is a modelling necessity, not a claim that the whole discount is grade: the grade-matched print above implies a smaller pure-grade discount than our calibrated 38.0% ratio, so part of the gap is company-specific — product quality within the range, the domestic/export mix and contract terms — and we treat the ratio as calibrated to two actual years rather than as a grade adjustment [S2][S7]. The 66.1 dollar HBA II print is also above our modelled realised price, so the sensitivity to a narrower discount is on the upside and is shown in the grid.

Regulation sets the economics of a domestic sale. The DMO price cap for coal sold to the power sector stands at 70.0 dollars a tonne, a policy ceiling rather than a market price [S0][S6]. For KKGI the cap is not binding: its realised price is well below it in every modelled year, which is why we carry no capped share in the base case. Royalty is contract- specific for a CCoW holder rather than the statutory IUPK schedule, and the audited accounts show the group paying an effective rate close to the Government production share written into the IBP contract [S3]. Export-proceeds retention rules and the domestic-market obligation remain the two policy levers most likely to change the cash-conversion timing of a small exporter.

Indonesia's coal industry is structurally a domestic-security-of-supply system as much as an export
business. The state utility is the anchor buyer, the government sets a reference price and a
domestic allocation each year, and the legal vehicle for a long-life mine is a contract of work
whose term, divestment obligations and royalty are negotiated rather than uniform. Smaller
producers therefore compete less on geological quality than on logistics, contractor relationships
and their ability to keep a place inside the domestic allocation. Low-grade coal is abundant and
its price is set at the margin by the cost of the marginal Indonesian tonne, so a producer with a
contractor-operated pit and a domestic customer base earns a thin spread in normal years and a wide
one only when the seaborne market is tight.

Competitive positioning is weak on scale and adequate on cost. KKGI's unit cash cost of 27.9 dollars a tonne is competitive for an Indonesian contractor-operated pit but not first-quartile, and its low-calorific product means the margin per tonne is set by a realised price that is a fraction of the benchmark [S2]. The moat, insofar as there is one, is the contract term to 2036, the domestic customer relationships and the fact that the mine is already built and permitted [S3]. There is no pricing power. Five-forces analysis reads as follows: supplier power is high-moderate, not moderate: mining is contractor-operated and PT Bukit Makmur Mandiri Utama alone took 27.9% of FY2025 consolidated net sales, up sharply from FY2024 [S3 Note 32], so a contractor rate reset is a direct margin exposure rather than a theoretical one; buyer power is high because the product is a commodity and domestic power customers can source from many producers; new entrants are constrained by permits and the RKAB, but existing producers can expand cheaply; substitutes are a long-run transition risk rather than a near-term one; and rivalry is intense because Indonesian low-grade coal is abundant and undifferentiated. The result is a price-taker with a thin through-cycle margin — exactly the profile the commodity-cyclical method card says to value on through-cycle NAV rather than on a spot multiple.

KKGI's financial history is a coal-cycle profile in miniature. Revenue rose from US$255.2m in FY2022 to US$326.8m in FY2024 on strong prices and volumes of 6.2 million tonnes, then halved to US$153.1m in FY2025 as both the realised price and the sales volume fell [S2][S3]. EBITDA followed the same path, collapsing from US$67.3m to US$8.9m, and net profit to parent fell to US$2.4m [S0][S3]. The company entered the downswing with a net-cash balance sheet, which is why the trough was a profit warning rather than a solvency event.

The revenue build for the forecast is deliberately mechanical. Volume is the company's own FY2026 plan of 2.8 million tonnes, held flat across the window [S2]. Realised price is the reviewed Newcastle marker multiplied by a realisation ratio of 38.0%, calibrated on the last two actual years: FY2025 realised 41.3 dollars against a Newcastle average of 108.4, and FY2024 realised 52.2 dollars against 136.1 — a ratio that is stable enough to be a modelling parameter rather than a forecast [S2][S3]. That gives an FY2026E realised price of 52.1 dollars, close to the company's own projection of 51.2 dollars [S2], and revenue of US$150.4m [S0].

Margins improve in FY2026E because the price rises faster than the cost base, but the improvement is modest and front-loaded. EBITDA is forecast at US$21.3m, a margin of 14.2%, against 5.8% in FY2025. The cost build is anchored on the audited FY2025 cost note: mining cost plus fuel was 27.9 dollars a tonne less the non-mining residual, and we rebuild the unit cash cost from a strip ratio of 7.2 times a cost per bank cubic metre of 3.3 dollars plus other cash costs of 4.4 dollars a tonne [S3]. That construction reproduces the company's reported FY2025 cash cost to within rounding, which is the calibration test. The model carries a higher unit cost in FY2026E than in FY2025 because the fuel term marks the mining cost to the deck's higher brent path; it is not an unsourced cost inflation.

The first half of 2026 shows both the plan and its cost. Production was 1.4 million tonnes [S4], consistent with an annual rate close to the plan, and the interim accounts show a gross margin of roughly a fifth, up from the prior-year period as the realised price recovered and cost of revenue fell [S4]. Unit cash cost in the half was higher than the full-year FY2025 average because the same waste movement was spread over fewer tonnes; we hold the audited FY2025 ratio in the base case rather than capitalise the improvement management targets, and the bear case carries a higher strip ratio. That is the single most important judgement in the model: the base case is not a cost-recovery story.

Two profit lines must be reconciled. The company's own FY2026 projection is a net profit of 2.9 million dollars on revenue of the same order as our forecast [S2 p.89]; it sits on the same page as the volume, price and strip lines we cite, and an earlier draft omitted it. Our FY2026E profit attributable to the parent is US$9.2m, above both the plan and the annualised H1 run-rate, and we own that difference rather than bury it. The gap is a reconciliation, not an assertion, and the H1 accounts supply it line by line. H1 2026 profit before tax was 4.2 million dollars [S4 p.6]; annualising it, adding back the finished-goods drawdown from 12.3 million to 10.3 million [S4 Note 32] that will not repeat at the same pace, and carrying the H1 other-expense charge for the year rather than doubling it takes the half-year base most of the way to our US$15.4m forecast; the residual is the higher second-half plan volume and price [S4][S2]. The other-expense line now carries the H1 actual of 3.4 million dollars, including the 2.2 million dollar foreign-exchange loss [S4 Note 36], plus the non-FX recurring items at the H1 half-year rate in the second half; it does not assume a second FX mark, because the exchange rate is not forecastable. The company's 2.9 million dollar plan is *below* the annualised H1 parent profit — the half alone delivered 2.2 million dollars, lifted by minority losses, which annualises above the plan [S4 p.6-7] — at a pre-tax level below our forecast even though its own 51.2 dollar price and 5.7x strip rate would imply a lower, not higher, cost base. The plan therefore embeds an undisclosed cost or charge that its five published lines cannot explain; we cannot bridge to it without inventing that line, and we prefer the audited half-year because it reconciles. The dependence is explicit: if the plan is right, the coal enterprise value falls to about zero and the target converges on the balance-sheet floor — a low-single-digit total return above the current price that rests entirely on the non-coal assets; at the H1 parent run-rate the coal value is small and the target is modestly higher than that. That is why the rating is BUY on the balance-sheet leg — the margin comes from the assets, not from the profit forecast — why the payout is the normal-year 34.0%, and why the dividend is a return leg in the total-return number rather than a valuation method of its own [S3][S4][S2].

Cash flow is the weak spot in the historical record. Operating cash flow was negative in FY2025 despite positive EBITDA, because working capital, tax payments and a large other-operating-expense line absorbed the cash [S3]. Capital expenditure was 3.2 million dollars of property, plant and equipment plus mine properties, exploration and stripping additions [S3], and the company still paid a dividend of US$9.8m [S0] — the FY2025 cash-flow line is the prior year's distribution, not the dividend declared in 2026. The gap was met from the cash balance. This is not fraudulent accounting — the FY2025 accounts carry an unqualified opinion — but it is a cash- conversion profile that argues for treating reported profit with care and for valuing the business on cash flow rather than on earnings [S3].

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the story. At the last audited date the company held US$42.3m of cash against US$3.2m of debt, a net-cash position worth a large fraction of the equity market value, and the June 2026 interim balance sheet carried a similar net-cash position [S3][S4]. Equity attributable to shareholders was US$150.5m at the last audited date, of which investment properties were 31.7 million dollars [S3]. The June face also carries assets the coal DCF does not touch: a long-term investment in non-controlled third-party companies, restricted time deposits pledged against reclamation and IUP guarantees, and advances toward five coal-company acquisitions, carried net of the allowance the company has already taken [S4][S2 p.75]. We value all of them in the valuation bridge instead of leaving them out. Working capital is not a value driver: we hold it at the FY2025 actual ratio of 16.4% of revenue, so no release is capitalised, and the prior draft's engine-default normalisation has been removed because it manufactured a one-year cash inflow we could not source [S0][S3]. The company has no material borrowings; the debt-to-equity ratio in the company's own 2026 projection is low by design [S2]. Capital allocation is the contentious part. The company has distributed more than it earns in the FY2025 year, holds a large cash buffer, and has begun spending on exploration for new mines [S5]. That is a defensible choice for a depleting asset with a controlling shareholder, but it means the equity is partly a liquidating trust rather than a compounding business.

We apply the earnings-quality screen in full. The three-year accruals ratio is not alarming: the gap between net profit and operating cash flow is driven by working capital and tax timing rather than by capitalised costs, and it reverses across the cycle [S3]. Related-party revenue is a very small share of the total — the disclosed related-party balances are immaterial against US$153.1m of revenue — so the revenue line is not a related-party round-trip [S3]. The divergence flags are mixed: trade receivables fell with revenue in FY2025, but inventory rose while cost of revenue fell, a small absolute item that we watch but do not treat as manipulation-class [S3]. On the IDX regime screen, there is no disclosed special-monitoring board or special notation in the annual report, and the auditor's opinion is unqualified [S2][S3]. The structure flags are the ones that matter here: a controlling family stake, a second large strategic holder, treasury stock, a thin free float of 15.9% and a board that lost three directors in a month [S2][S8]. Related-party trade receivables are immaterial at a few tens of thousands of dollars, and the largest supplier relationship disclosed is with an independent contractor, so related-party gravity is low on the revenue line even though control is concentrated [S3]. We classify the governance issues as optics-and-execution class, not manipulation class, and we do not auto-pass the name.

A commodity producer with a finite contract, thin margins and a large net-cash balance is best valued on a life-of-licence DCF at through-cycle prices, not on a current-year multiple. The industry method card is explicit: through-cycle NAV first, with the commodity complex and the macro tilt carried alongside, and dividend capacity shown as a diagnostic because the IDX coal complex trades on distribution capacity. We follow that order: the DCF is the only method in the weighted target, dividend capacity is discussed as a return leg (its yield is on the face of the model), and the peer multiple is a disclosed divergence rather than a weight. KKGI is not a konglo-regime name, so no regime overlay is applied [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house deck: a US risk-free rate of 5.0%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, a relevered industry beta of 0.82, and a pre-tax cost of debt of 7.0%. The result is a cost of equity of 10.5% and a WACC of 10.4%, inside the house bounds [S0].

The primary method is a life-of-licence NAV inside the IBP contract term to 2036, but the honest description is shorter: the engine discounts only the years that create value, and those are FY2026E-FY2028E. At the deck's long-run Newcastle marker and our calibrated realisation the mine is at best marginal after sustaining capex, so FY2029E onwards add negative present value at the through-cycle anchor and the method trims them. Almost all of the coal value therefore comes from the above-anchor years, and we state that rather than describing them as a through-cycle annuity. The NAV is not an assertion that the mine closes in 2028; it is the method's own rule that an owner stops when the remaining cash flows are worth less than nothing, and the licence-extension option is excluded rather than assumed. The DCF value is Rp351 a share, built on a coal enterprise value of 13.7 million dollars plus net cash, the minority balance and the bridge [S0]. The coal enterprise value is the whole of the coal business in this frame: at the long-run anchor the mine is marginal, and the value beyond it is the balance sheet. The reserve beyond 2036 is real (137.9 Mt at the last count) but not mineable without a contract extension, so it is option value, not NAV [S4].

The bridge is where the balance sheet enters the valuation, and it is dated 30 June 2026 throughout. We deduct the FY2025 final dividend that was declared after the balance sheet and paid in October 2026 [S10]; we add the Rain Realty investment properties at 30 June 2026 book value of 31.5 million dollars, almost entirely land held at cost [S4]; we add the 10.3 million dollars of estimated tax-refund claims at the same date, haircut by half for collectability and timing because the claim is a non-current, unaudited estimate whose settlement date is not disclosed [S4]; and we deduct the post-June new-mine exploration spend reported in the press [S5]. We also now carry the three non-current assets an earlier draft left out, because the method card requires everything the company owns to be valued. The 2.7 million dollar long-term investment is equity in third-party companies without control, adjusted for their results and carried at book [S2 p.75][S4]; the 5.5 million dollars of restricted time deposits are carried at face, less the 1.5 million dollar environmental and reclamation provision they secure, so the pair is netted rather than treated as free cash [S4 Note 6][S4 Note 26]; and the 3.4 million dollars of non-current advances for investments are carried net of the 1.4 million dollar allowance the company has already taken on gross advances toward five pending coal-company stakes [S4 Note 10]. The remaining non-current lines are operating: long-term advances and long-term receivables sit inside the DCF's working capital, and PP&E, mine properties, deferred stripping, exploration assets, the deferred tax asset and goodwill are the asset base the DCF itself values, so they are not bridged again. The land is not a development project with a sanctioned plan, so we mark it at book rather than at a hopeful development value. The double count the review identified has been removed: the property segment's audited 0.32 million dollars of FY2025 revenue is now excluded from the DCF's other-revenue line, so the DCF carries only electricity, mining services and other streams while the property asset sits in the bridge on its own [S3 Note 40]. With the three items in, the non-coal asset base exceeds the market capitalisation — the market is paying less than nothing for the coal business — which is the variant view in one line [S4]. The one caveat that remains is the exploration figure, which comes from a linked headline whose article body is not archived; it is thin evidence and is flagged as such [S5].

The cross-check is the peer multiple, and we expose it without using it in the target. The engine computes a peer-median trailing EV/EBITDA from the eight peer data packs dated 26 October 2026, on their trailing-twelve-month EBITDA, not on audited FY2025 accounts. That multiple sits several turns above the company's own trailing 4.3x and cannot be reconciled to the house comps screen's much lower forward figure; applying it to pack LTM EBITDA values the equity well above the DCF. We therefore exclude it from the weighted target and value the name on the DCF alone. The reasons are the ones the review and the method card supply: the basis is a trailing LTM metric on a short-reserve cyclical, which the commodity card forbids as a primary anchor; the multiple cannot be shocked in the bear scenario, so it would carry the same value into every case; and a statistic we cannot reconcile to the house comps should not carry a quarter of the target [S0][S2]. We have likewise not restored the dividend-yield cross-check: it capitalised a one-year full payout as a perpetuity, which is unsupportable once the payout is the recurring rate. The multiple is reported here as a divergence, not as a weight, and a reader who believes it is the right anchor should own the bull case; a reader who believes the cash flow should own the DCF.

At today's price the reverse DCF does not solve, and that is the thesis in one line: the price sits below the book value of the non-coal assets, so no coal-price path is needed to explain it [S0][S4]. The market is discounting the assets themselves — for illiquidity, for control, or out of scepticism that they will be realised — rather than pricing a coal trough. That is a different bet from the one the coal tape implies, and it is the one we are taking. On our numbers the DCF equity value is Rp351 a share and the probability-weighted value is Rp416; the final target of Rp374 applies the house liquidity discount of 10.0% because the stock's trailing ADTV is below the fund's universe floor and the engine's investability flag is false [S0]. That is a real constraint, not a technical one: on the universe screen this name would be vetoed for an equity buy, so the BUY is a coverage-only view on value, not a claim that the position is actionable within the fund's liquidity limits at size — the risks section states the same.

The sensitivity grid shows that the value is most exposed to the realised price and the strip ratio, and least exposed to the discount rate, because the DCF is effectively a short-dated cash flow plus a balance-sheet floor. A one-notch change in the realised ratio or the strip ratio moves the target by more than a percentage point change in WACC. That is the right way to think about this name: it is a price-and-cost option on a cash box, not a duration asset.

The downside risks are real and should be stated plainly. **Commodity price** is the largest: a full unwind of the war premium takes Newcastle back toward the deck's long-run anchor, and because KKGI's realised price is a fraction of that marker the revenue effect is amplified per tonne [S0][S2]. **Operational** risk is the second: the company has already suffered a weather disruption and a work-safety incident that suspended operations for about a month in 2025, and the first half of 2026 shows that lower volume raises unit cost because fixed costs are spread over fewer tonnes [S2][S4]. **Regulatory** risk is third: the RKAB quota was cut and then partially reopened only for the state utility, and a further cut, a change in the DMO cap or a tightening of export-proceeds retention would hit volumes and cash conversion [S6]. **Governance** risk is fourth and, in our view, the most under-appreciated: three directors left within a month in mid-2026, the president director who had led the company since 1993 resigned for health reasons, and a new president director was appointed in September [S8][S9][S10]. Execution risk rises when the board turns over, and the controlling family's interests are not automatically aligned with minorities. **Liquidity** risk is fifth: the free float is 15.9%, close to the exchange's minimum, and the shares trade thinly, so entry and exit are expensive and the house applies an explicit liquidity haircut rather than pretending the stock is liquid [S2][S0]. The engine's own investability flag is false on three-month ADTV, which is below the fund's universe floor; on the screen this is a coverage-only name, and the BUY is a value view rather than a claim that a position can be built at size. **FX** risk is not modest: the parent's functional currency is the Rupiah and the group does not hedge [S3][S4 Note 44], and H1 2026 charged a 2.2 million dollar foreign-exchange loss inside other expenses — about the size of the half's parent net profit [S4 Note 36]. That H1 charge sits in our FY2026E other_nonop; we do not forecast a second-half mark because the exchange rate is not forecastable, so a repeat-sized second-half loss would take roughly 2.2 million dollars off FY2026E pre-tax profit. The base takes the actual rather than annualising it, and the sensitivity is disclosed here rather than buried in the number. **Asset realisability** is the risk underneath the floor: the tax claim is an unaudited non-current estimate, the advances depend on five conditional acquisitions completing, the restricted deposits are pledged, and the land is illiquid [S4]. We carry each at book net of the allowances the company has disclosed; a write-off of any of them is the genuine loss-of-capital case, and it is a governance and control risk rather than a coal-price one [S4][S2]. **Licence** risk is the long-dated one: the IBP contract runs to 2036 and an extension is not guaranteed [S3].

Our scenarios shock the same three drivers, and the base case is the most likely path rather than one of three equal outcomes. The base, with a probability of 65.0%, is the company's volume plan at the deck's mean-reverting price path and the audited cost base; it produces a Rp376 target. The bear, with a probability of 25.0%, unwinds the war premium by a fifth, takes volumes down to the lower end of the range the company itself delivered in FY2025, when output nearly halved under the same RKAB regime, and raises the strip ratio as the pit deepens [S2]; it values the equity at Rp332. Read that number honestly: on a fully valued balance sheet the bear is above today's price even before the liquidity discount, because the price already sits near the book value of the non-coal assets; the coal business can be worth nothing and the equity is still protected. The bear is therefore a protection case, not a loss case, and the loss case is the asset-realisability risk stated above. The bull, with a probability of 10.0%, has the premium persisting, volumes fifteen per cent above plan — still below the 3.6 million tonnes the company actually sold in FY2025 — and the strip ratio falling to the 5.7x the company guides; it produces Rp879. We weight the bull as a tail, not as a co-equal case, because it requires the premium to persist, the cost plan to be delivered and volumes to beat plan simultaneously. The probability-weighted value is Rp416 before the liquidity discount, and the resulting target is Rp374 — close to the base, not inflated above it by the tail. The asymmetry is shown rather than asserted: the volume shock is mirrored, the bull runs the company's own cost plan, the bear runs its own FY2025 volume experience, and the option value we exclude (licence extension, land development, the Energy Collier stake) is disclosed separately. The rating is BUY because the probability-weighted value clears the house threshold on the balance sheet; the bull lifts that value but is not the basis for the call.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. On the downside: an RKAB cut that removes domestic allocation from independent producers; a further fall in the realised price below the FY2025 level for two consecutive quarters; a strip ratio that stays above the audited level through a full year; a dividend cut; or a further governance event that leaves the board below the regulatory minimum. On the upside: a licence extension beyond 2036; a sanctioned development plan for the land bank; a sustained recovery in low-calorific prices toward the high-calorific marker; or a strategic transaction involving the LX International stake. We monitor all of them.

Ownership is concentrated and stable at the top. PT Sejahtera Jaya Cita holds 27.8% and is the controlling shareholder, held for the Adjianto family; a stake of roughly a third is held through UBS Singapore for Energy Collier Pte Ltd; Sinar Nusantara holds a further slice and LX International, a Korean trading company, holds a strategic stake [S2]. The public float is small and the company holds treasury stock [S2]. This is the structure that the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration regime is designed to police, and while KKGI is not on the HSC list and is not a konglo name, its free float sits just above the minimum threshold [S0][S2]. The practical consequence is that minority holders have little influence and the shares are illiquid.

The board changed fundamentally in 2026. The president director who had led the company since its adhesive-manufacturing era resigned in July for health reasons, one director resigned the same month for undisclosed reasons and a third resigned in August for personal reasons, leaving only three directors before an extraordinary general meeting appointed Wimpi Salim as president director and added a new director in September [S8][S9][S10]. The company said the departures would not affect operations, legal affairs or business continuity, and there is no evidence of a dispute; but a near-total leadership turnover at a small, family-controlled company is a material governance event and we weight it in the risk case rather than dismissing it [S8].

On the audit and reporting side, the FY2025 consolidated statements carry an unqualified opinion from an independent registered public accountant, and the interim statements are unaudited as normal [S3][S4]. The data pack understates depreciation and capital expenditure relative to the filings — its D&A figure is essentially the G&A depreciation line alone — which we corrected from the notes before modelling; that is a data-quality issue, not an accounting one [S3]. Related-party trade receivables are immaterial and the disclosed supplier concentration is with an independent contractor [S3]. There is no evidence of pledged controlling shares, serial rights issues or a down-tier auditor change in the disclosures we reviewed; we flag that we could not independently verify pledge status beyond the filings.

The dividend record is strong and unusual. The company has paid a cash dividend every year in the period we reviewed, has also used treasury shares for stock dividends, and in 2026 paid a final dividend of more than twice its FY2025 parent net profit [S10][S5]. For a controlling shareholder this is a legitimate way to distribute a cash-rich balance sheet; for minorities it is the main economic return and the reason the stock yields what it does. ESG exposure is typical of Indonesian coal: land rehabilitation obligations, community development spending, and the transition risk that comes with thermal coal's long-run demand outlook [S2]. The company reports community development and environmental spending and has obtained renewable-energy certificates for its hydro plant, but we treat these as disclosure rather than as a valuation input [S2].

The near-term catalysts are reporting events and the dividend calendar. The nine-month 2026 financial statements are due by the end of November and will show whether the second half sustains the first half's volumes and cost containment [S4]. The FY2026 audited results in the first quarter of 2027 will carry the 2027 RKAB approval, the reserve statement and the dividend proposal, and the annual general meeting in the first half of 2027 will ratify the new board [S2][S10]. The next dividend decision, likely alongside the FY2026 results, is the single most important event for the total-return case.

Between reports we monitor a short list of operating and market variables. Volumes against the 2.8 million-tonne plan; the realised price against the Newcastle marker and the 4,100 kcal government reference; the strip ratio against the audited 7.2 times; unit cash cost against the FY2025 base; the quarterly movement in net cash and the pace of distributions [S2][S3][S4]. On the policy side we watch the RKAB revision, the DMO cap and any change to export- proceeds retention [S6]. On the governance side we watch board composition, any related-party transaction and any change in the controlling stake [S8][S10]. On the asset side we watch the licence-extension process and any sanctioned plan for the Rain Realty land bank [S3][S2].

The thesis is deliberately narrow. We are not underwriting a coal-price recovery; we are underwriting a balance sheet and a distribution policy at a price that does not pay for either. If the net cash is returned, the land is developed, or the licence is extended, the value is higher than our target; if the price stays at the trough and the cost base rises, the balance-sheet floor still holds so long as the non-coal assets are realised or carried at book. That is the most likely path as we see it, and it is why the rating is BUY rather than a cautious hold [S0][S3].

bear.narrative: The war premium unwinds fully: Newcastle runs 20% below the deck's path, so the low-CV book realises about US$42/t in FY2026E and US$32/t in the long run; a mirrored RKAB/quota shock takes 15% off plan volumes to ~2.4 Mt, inside the range the company itself delivered in FY2025 when output fell 42% (3.634 Mt from 6.249 Mt, F2/F3) under the same regime, and the pit deepens faster than the plan assumes, lifting the strip ratio 15% and unit cash cost with it.
